name: Acadian Museum of Erath (D.L. Menard exhibit)
writeup: The Acadian Museum, founded in 1990, has a large Cajun music exhibit centered on Erath's own D.L. Menard. Born outside town in 1932, Menard moved into Erath at sixteen, heard live Cajun music for the first time and ordered an eleven-dollar guitar from a catalog. He was soon playing dances with Elias Badeaux and the Louisiana Aces. In 1961, between customers at the service station where he worked, he wrote La Porte d'en Arrière (The Back Door), which earned back its recording cost within days and became a Cajun standard. He later built ash rocking chairs in a shop beside his house and was named a National Heritage Fellow in 1994.

name: Club Rumors (Club Discovery)
writeup: This two-story building on St. Claude Avenue opened as the nightclub Club Discovery in 1988 and was renamed Club Rumors in 1993. It held a thousand people or more on weekend nights. When bounce appeared in 1991, the year used here, DJ Captain Charles broke the new records from its booth, and dance contests gave young performers a stage. KLC, who took over as DJ in 1993, tested his own productions on the crowd before Master P recruited him for No Limit; Mannie Fresh of Cash Money worked the same room. After shootings in 1997 the state revoked the club's license in 1998. The building still stands.

name: Ghost Town Lounge
writeup: Bounce, New Orleans's own form of hip-hop, is usually traced to this small bar in Hollygrove, in the 17th Ward. In 1991 MC T. Tucker and DJ Irv Phillips performed here over a loop from the Showboys' "Drag Rap," the beat locals call Triggerman, with Tucker calling out nearby neighborhoods and the crowd shouting back. A cassette of the routine, "Where Dey At," known as the red tape, is widely considered the first bounce release. The call-and-response chants and that beat became the template for DJ Jimi, Cash Money's early records and, later, Big Freedia. The building is no longer in use as a club.

name: Magnolia Projects (C.J. Peete) and Cash Money Records
writeup: The C.J. Peete public housing development, built in Central City in 1939 and known to everyone as the Magnolia, became the best-known address in New Orleans hip-hop. Brothers Bryan "Baby" Williams and Ronald "Slim" Williams started Cash Money Records around 1991 and tied the label to the complex. Juvenile and Turk of the Hot Boys grew up there, and Juvenile's 1998 video for "Ha" showed it to the country. Soulja Slim began rapping here as Magnolia Slim in 1993, and bounce artist Magnolia Shorty carried its name. The City Council voted in 2007 to demolish the complex; the mixed-income Harmony Oaks development now stands on the site.

name: Peaches Records, Gentilly Boulevard (former store)
writeup: Shirani Rea's record shop opened on Gentilly Boulevard by 1984; it is mapped here from 1991, when bounce began and the store became its main counter. A Times-Picayune writer called it the epicenter of the bounce craze, reporting that local bounce tapes outsold national rap stars there ten to one. Mia X worked the register from 1990 and sold thousands of copies of her own answer record, "Da Payback." Master P and the Cash Money owners dealt with Rea directly, and Mannie Fresh tried out new tracks on her customers. The store flooded after Hurricane Katrina; Peaches now trades on Magazine Street.

name: Wetlands Acadian Cultural Center
writeup: This National Park Service center on the bank of Bayou Lafourche, part of Jean Lafitte National Historical Park and Preserve, tells the story of the Acadians who settled Louisiana's bayous. It occupies the Percy-Lobdell Building, a 1907 grocery warehouse that was renovated and given a 200-seat theater before opening to the public in 1992. Music has long been part of the program: local players have gathered here for free jam sessions, held for years on Monday evenings and at times on Saturday mornings, and the center has hosted outdoor Cajun and zydeco concerts. It gives the bayou parishes, east of the Cajun prairie, a public home for the music.

name: Choctaw-Apache Tribe of Ebarb Pow Wow Grounds
writeup: The Choctaw-Apache Tribe of Ebarb, recognized by Louisiana in 1978, is the state's second-largest tribe, with more than seven thousand citizens, half of them in Sabine Parish. A 2014 news report counted that spring's powwow as the tribe's twenty-first annual gathering, which would put the first around 1994; since 2011 it has been held on permanent tribal grounds near Zwolle, mapped here. The tribe describes the annual Pow Wow as a celebration of culture, tradition and living Indigenous presence, with intertribal dancing, drum groups, Native artisans and shared food. The community traces its roots to eighteenth-century Spanish and French colonial settlements, including Los Adaes, and members are again studying their ancestral languages and practicing traditional social dances.

name: Calliope Projects (B.W. Cooper) and No Limit Records
writeup: The B.W. Cooper public housing development, built between 1939 and 1941 and always called the Calliope, raised two generations of New Orleans musicians. The Neville brothers, pianist Willie Tee, the Dixie Cups and Henry Butler all lived here. Percy Miller, known as Master P, was raised in the Calliope by his grandparents, started No Limit Records in California, and moved the label to New Orleans around 1995. With his brothers C-Murder and Silkk the Shocker he made the project's name familiar to rap listeners nationwide, and No Limit sold more than fifty million albums by 2001. The complex flooded in 2005 and had been demolished by 2014, except for three brick buildings.

name: Ernie K-Doe's Mother-in-Law Lounge
writeup: Ernie K-Doe's "Mother-in-Law" topped the national pop and rhythm and blues charts in May 1961. By the 1980s he was better known in New Orleans for his outlandish, free-associating radio shows on WWOZ. In 1995 Antoinette Fox, whom he later married, opened this lounge on North Claiborne Avenue, and it gave the self-styled Emperor of the Universe a stage and a late revival. After he died on July 5, 2001, Antoinette kept it going, with a dressed mannequin of her husband on display, through the 2005 flood and until her own death on Mardi Gras Day 2009. The lounge closed in 2010. Trumpeter Kermit Ruffins reopened it in 2014; in September 2026 he announced he was giving it up.

name: Tunica-Biloxi Pow Wow
writeup: Each spring the Tunica-Biloxi Tribe of Louisiana hosts a Pow Wow on its reservation at Marksville. The tribe counted its 2010 gathering as the fifteenth and, after three years lost to the pandemic, its 2026 gathering as the twenty-eighth, which puts the first in 1996; John Barbry, the committee's longtime chairman, dated the present form to 1995 and said a summer Green Corn festival came before it. Dancers from many Native nations take part in inter-tribal dances and judged competitions, alongside traditional Tunica-Biloxi songs and dances, storytelling and Native flute. The tribe describes the event as a way to honor its ancestors, strengthen ties among its citizens and guests, and show that Native people and their traditions are still present.

name: Cajun French Music Hall of Fame and Museum
writeup: The Cajun French Music Association, a nonprofit founded in 1984 to promote and preserve Cajun music, keeps its hall of fame at 240 South C.C. Duson Street, a block from the Liberty Theatre. The museum opened on November 29, 1997, in a one-room country store building from the 1930s, and the first inductees were announced that day; the list now runs past one hundred musicians nominated by the association's chapters. Inside are fiddles, accordions, guitars, hats and belts that belonged to them, some of the earliest Cajun records, and old dance hall advertisements. Many of those honored played on front porches and in small halls before the music was fashionable. Admission is free.

name: The Jolly Inn
writeup: The Jolly Inn on Barrow Street opened in 1998 and took its name from an older dance hall near Houma where founder Werlien Prosperie had gone with his parents as a boy and later played guitar and sang. Prosperie, who played accordion in a band called Couche Couche, built the new hall around live Cajun bands, and his daughter Sonia McNamara took it over. Dances on Friday nights and Sunday afternoons run through two-steps, waltzes, line dances and swamp pop. The family has said it may be the only dance hall left between New Orleans and Lafayette.

name: Backstreet Cultural Museum
writeup: Sylvester Francis began filming second lines, jazz funerals and Carnival in Tremé around 1970. In 1999 he opened this museum in a former funeral home in the neighborhood to hold his photographs and films along with Mardi Gras Indian suits and objects from jazz funerals and second line parades. It works as much as a meeting place as a gallery: the Northside Skull and Bone Gang sets out from it on Mardi Gras morning, Indian gangs gather there, and the museum hosts an All Saints' Day procession meant to keep the jazz funeral alive. After Hurricane Ida damaged the original building in 2021, the museum moved in 2022 to St. Philip Street.

name: Blue Moon Saloon and Guesthouse
writeup: The Blue Moon is a bar, stage and dance floor attached to a guesthouse at 215 East Convent Street in Lafayette's Freetown neighborhood. Mark Falgout has owned and run it since 2001, and it has become a regular stop for local and touring roots bands, with live Cajun music, a standing Cajun jam and heavy crowds during Festival International. Travelers staying in the guesthouse share the place with the dancers, which gives it a reputation as a honky-tonk where visitors and locals mix. Listed for sale in January 2025, the property was sold in 2026 to investor Ken Simeral under a leaseback that keeps Falgout running the venue.

name: Delta Music Museum and Arcade Theater
writeup: Ferriday, a small town in Concordia Parish, produced three cousins who became famous in three different fields: rock and roll pianist Jerry Lee Lewis, country star Mickey Gilley and television evangelist Jimmy Swaggart. This museum on Louisiana Avenue, set up in 2001 by a local friends group and the state and run by the Louisiana Secretary of State's office, tells their story and honors some thirty blues, gospel, soul and country artists from the delta region. Exhibits also recall Haney's Big House, the Ferriday club on the chitlin' circuit that burned in 1966. The adjoining Arcade Theater hosts live performances.

name: Abita Springs Opry (Abita Springs Town Hall)
writeup: Six times a year the old wooden town hall in Abita Springs fills for the Abita Springs Opry, a concert series run by a nonprofit to preserve and present Louisiana roots music, played mostly acoustically. Since 2002 its programs have centered on old-time country, bluegrass and traditional Southern gospel, with Cajun, zydeco, Irish and traditional New Orleans jazz bands sharing the bill. The series has had a single cancellation, after Hurricane Katrina, and reached its hundredth show in 2019. The hall is more than a hundred years old, with pecky cypress walls, wooden floors and room for just under four hundred listeners.

name: House of Dance and Feathers
writeup: Ronald W. Lewis, who had been involved with Mardi Gras Indians since he was thirteen, began this museum in his garage in the Lower Ninth Ward in 2003. It holds photographs and objects from Mardi Gras Indian gangs, social aid and pleasure club second lines and Skull and Bone gangs, all explained from inside the culture; Lewis was president of the Big Nine Social Aid and Pleasure Club. The first building flooded when the Industrial Canal levee failed in 2005, and a new one went up behind his house the next year. Lewis died of COVID-19 in March 2020. His wife, Minnie Lewis, reopened the museum in December 2022.

name: Bois Sec Ardoin's grave, Ceaser Cemetery
writeup: Alphonse "Bois Sec" Ardoin was born in 1915 near Bayou Duralde, in a Creole farming settlement between Mamou and Basile, and never moved far from it. From 1948 he and fiddler Canray Fontenot played house dances as the Duralde Ramblers, keeping the old accordion and fiddle la-la alive; they appeared at the Newport Folk Festival in 1966 and were both named National Heritage Fellows in 1986. His son Morris ran Club Morris nearby, where the family band played. Ardoin died on May 16, 2007, and was buried in this country cemetery, which is why the point is dated from 2007.

name: The Roots of Music (Marching Crusaders campus)
writeup: Derrick Tabb, a drummer with the Rebirth Brass Band, started The Roots of Music in 2007 as a six-week summer drum camp at Tipitina's, after Hurricane Katrina left many New Orleans schools without music programs. It grew into a free, year-round program whose Marching Crusaders, aged nine to fourteen, receive instruments, tutoring, hot meals and bus rides, and it has sent its band to the Rose Parade. Tabb modeled it on the band he came up in at Bell Junior High. After about ten moves between borrowed and leased rooms, the organization bought the former St. Gabriel Catholic Church property on Piety Drive in June 2025. The map shows that campus, its first permanent home.

name: Tuba Fats Square
writeup: One evening in 2007, brass band musicians led mourners through Tremé to play for Kerwin James, a tuba player who had just died. Police answering a noise complaint sent more than twenty cars and took Derrick Tabb and Glen David Andrews away in handcuffs. Many saw it as an attack on a neighborhood custom generations old. In response the owner of this corner lot at St. Philip and North Robertson, with Tremé musicians, named it for Anthony "Tuba Fats" Lacen, the bandleader who taught so many young players, and set it aside for music. A Tuba Fats Tuesday festival has been held here since 2009.

name: Louisiana Swamp Pop Museum
writeup: Swamp pop is the rhythm-and-blues-flavored rock and roll that south Louisiana teenagers made their own in the late 1950s and early 1960s, trading the Cajun accordion and fiddle for electric guitars and horns. Ville Platte, where radio station KVPI pushed the new records, was proclaimed the Swamp Pop Capital of the World by the Louisiana Legislature, and in 2010 this museum opened in the town's old train depot. It displays stage costumes, photographs, records and a wall of autographs, and explains why so many performers took stage names, as Bobby Charles Guidry did for "See You Later, Alligator."

name: Robert Finley Marker (Bernice Depot Museum)
writeup: Blues and soul singer Robert Finley, born in 1954, comes from Winnsboro in Franklin Parish but has spent most of his life in Bernice, where he worked as a carpenter, played blues in juke joints and sang gospel in churches. He lost his sight at about sixty, which ended his woodworking business and left more time for music. His debut album, Age Don't Mean a Thing, appeared in 2016, the year used here, and later records were made with producer Dan Auerbach. He has since headlined festivals in Ireland and France. The Northeast Louisiana Music Trail unveiled his marker in front of the Bernice Depot Museum on September 20, 2025.
